text: This might be the single most important lesson in the whole course for separating a real quant from a hobbyist. The honest fact driving it: most backtested edges don't survive out-of-sample, and this lesson is the main reason why.

Data snooping is testing many ideas against the same historical data and reporting the best one as if it were a single test. Test a hundred meaningless random rules against five years of data, and pure chance guarantees some will show a great-looking Sharpe ratio — not because they're real, just because with enough tries you'll find something that happened to fit that sample's noise. It's the same logic as flipping a hundred coins and finding one that comes up heads most of the time.

Overfitting is that same problem happening inside one strategy's parameters. Sweep thousands of moving-average window combinations, keep whichever one scored best on the same data you searched, and that best score is the maximum of thousands of noisy samples — not an honest single sample. It's almost guaranteed to look good, whether or not there's a real signal underneath.

The defenses are disciplined, not clever. Hold out a real chunk of data — commonly the most recent twenty to thirty percent — and never touch it until the strategy is finished. Better yet, use walk-forward analysis: repeatedly re-fit on a rolling past window and test on what comes right after, rolling forward through time, which is much closer to how a real researcher actually has to operate. And keep the parameter search small — the more things you tried, the weaker your result's real statistical significance.

An in-sample Sharpe ratio that collapses out-of-sample is the single most reliable tell that you found an overfit artifact, not a durable edge — and it happens to careful professionals constantly.
